title: India Falls Behind Turkey in the Fifth-Generation Fighter Jet Race
excerpt: Turkey's KAAN fighter has completed ground tests of its second prototype, while India's AMCA programme is still years away from its first flight — but a private sector push could close the gap.
body:
• Turkey's KAAN P1 prototype completed powered taxi tests on July 31, 2026, with two prototypes expected to be airborne by year-end
  • India's AMCA is targeting a first prototype rollout by 2027 and maiden flight around 2028-2029, trailing Turkey by four to five years
  • India has opened the AMCA programme to private sector companies for the first time, issuing a ₹15,000 crore RFP to Tata, L&T-BEL, and Bharat Forge-BEML
  • Both nations are using interim American engines while developing indigenous powerplants, a pragmatic strategy that decouples airframe testing from engine development
  • South Korea's KF-21 has already entered production, putting India behind both Asian rivals and Turkey in the 5th-generation timeline

Turkey's fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet has crossed another milestone, completing powered taxi tests of its updated P1 prototype on July 31 — a development that throws into sharp relief just how far India's own stealth fighter programme has yet to go.

While Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) prepares to put a second and third prototype in the air by the end of 2026, India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) remains in the manufacturing phase, with its first prototype not expected until 2027 and a maiden flight targeted around 2028 or 2029.

Turkey's Aggressive Timeline

The KAAN programme has moved at a pace that has surprised defence analysts. The original P0 prototype made its maiden flight on February 21, 2024, completing a 13-minute flight to 8,000 feet from TAI's Ankara airfield. A second test flight followed in May 2024, reaching 10,000 feet.

The P1 prototype, which features aerodynamic and radar cross-section refinements over the P0, successfully concluded its ground evaluations on July 31, 2026. TUSAŞ aims to have both P1 and a subsequent P2 prototype airborne before year-end. In total, six prototypes are planned for the flight test programme.

"Instead of relying on a solitary demonstrator jet to sequentially clear every hurdle, TUSAŞ is operating multiple distinct prototypes at once — drastically shortening the development lifecycle."

— Defence News India analysis

Turkey's strategy of running overlapping prototypes — with P0 expanding its flight envelope while P1 undergoes ground integration and a structural model handles stress tests — has allowed the programme to accumulate test data far faster than a sequential approach would permit.

India's AMCA: Playing Catch-Up

India's AMCA programme tells a different story. Launched in 2010, the project received Cabinet Committee on Security approval in March 2024 with a budget of approximately ₹15,000 crore for the development phase. The Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) plans to build five prototypes rolled out in eight-to-nine-month intervals.

A full-scale aero model is currently undergoing radar cross-section testing at DRDO's Dundigal facility in Hyderabad — a critical milestone, but one that Turkey passed years ago. The AMCA's first flight remains at least two to three years away, with service entry projected around 2034-2035.

The comparison grows starker when South Korea's KF-21 Boramae is factored in. Having made its maiden flight in 2022, the KF-21 has already entered Block I production and is expected to be operational by 2026 — nearly a decade ahead of the AMCA.

The Engine Bottleneck

Both India and Turkey have adopted identical strategies to avoid the single biggest delay factor in fighter jet development: the engine. Turkey's initial KAAN prototypes fly on American General Electric F110 engines while Turkish firms develop the indigenous 35,000-pound-thrust TF35000 turbofan, expected to be integrated by roughly 2032.

India has taken the same approach, planning to fly its first AMCA prototypes on GE F414 engines while co-developing a 110-kilonewton engine with France's Safran through a joint venture with the Gas Turbine Research Establishment. That engine has a 10-year development timeline.

"By decoupling the airframe's testing schedule from the complex process of domestic engine development, both countries ensure their stealth jets can mature on a reliable foreign powerplant today, while securing self-reliance for tomorrow."

— Defence News India

Private Sector Shake-Up

India's most significant recent move has been opening the AMCA programme to the private sector. On May 27, 2026, the Ministry of Defence issued a Request for Proposal to three private sector groups: Tata Advanced Systems Limited, a Larsen & Toubro-BEL consortium, and a Bharat Forge-BEML group. For the first time in six decades, the lead integrator role is shifting away from state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.

This mirrors the commercially accountable model that has allowed TUSAŞ to execute the KAAN programme rapidly. Defence analysts see the private sector push as India's best chance of compressing its development timeline and bringing competitive urgency to a programme that has historically moved at a bureaucratic pace.

What's Next

Turkey is targeting an initial service entry for the KAAN's Block 10 variant by 2028-2029. India's AMCA, if current timelines hold, will not enter service until the mid-2030s. The gap is significant, but India's proponents argue that the combination of private sector involvement, proven interim engines, and DRDO's stealth testing infrastructure gives the programme a credible path forward — provided execution matches ambition.
image_caption: Turkey's KAAN fifth-generation fighter jet during testing. The programme has moved rapidly from maiden flight in 2024 to multiple prototype ground tests in 2026.
nri_angle: India's defence self-reliance efforts, including the AMCA programme, are closely watched by the diaspora as markers of national technological progress. The private sector opening also creates potential opportunities for diaspora professionals in defence technology.
